figures.headline: At batch size 16384, cuPIQP's dense and sparse backends solve the IK and WBC batches faster than the baseline solvers.

figures.headline: Learned MPC weights cut root-mean-square position error from 187 mm to 55 mm, with nearly identical loss curves across solvers.
citing_sentences: After training, the root-mean-square (RMS) position error decreases from $187\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ to $55\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}$ with the learned weights for all five solvers, as illustrated by Fig. 2(a).
Moreover, the loss curves versus Adam step nearly coincide across solvers as shown in Fig. 2(b).
The solvers therefore achieve essentially the same control performance and differ primarily in computational time, as shown in Fig. 2(c).

abstract: Quadratic programs (QPs) are fundamental building blocks of many robotic tasks such as inverse kinematics, whole-body control, and model predictive control. Extending these methods to large-scale robot learning and control requires solving many QPs concurrently and, for end-to-end learning, differentiating through their solutions. Efficient batched optimization is therefore essential to bringing established model-based methods into GPU-based robotics pipelines. We present cuPIQP, a batched and differentiable QP solver on GPUs based on a proximal interior-point method, with unified support for dense, sparse, and multistage problems. The solver exploits parallelism across independent QPs and their internal structure while preserving per-problem numerical updates and termination decisions. Benchmarks with up to 16384 QPs per batch demonstrate solve-time speedups of up to $18.8\times$ over Moreau and $4.26\times$ over eight-core PIQP. In an end-to-end learning task, cuPIQP accelerates training by $4.6\times$ over QPAX and $7.8\times$ over Moreau. By reducing the computational cost, cuPIQP provides efficient, reusable infrastructure for integrating model-based optimization into large-scale robot learning and control.

sections.body: The introduction states that existing QP solvers, such as qpOASES, OSQP, HPIPM, ProxQP and PIQP, minimize latency for one or a few problems. Learning and control workloads instead solve a batch of $B$ independent QPs that share dimensions and sparsity patterns but differ in numerical data, so throughput matters. QP data often live on the GPU, and a CPU solver adds transfers and synchronization. Prior GPU solvers target single large sparse problems, treat batches through block-diagonal assembly, or specialize to one structure (QPTH, QPAX, Moreau). The stated contributions are batch-native execution with per-problem iterates and termination, dense, sparse and multistage backends, and GPU-resident implicit differentiation.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing QP solvers target single-problem latency, so batched learning workloads need a GPU-native batched solver.

sections.body: The section recalls the proximal interior-point method of PIQP for one QP. Slack variables turn the inequalities into equalities, and a proximal method of multipliers is applied to an augmented Lagrangian, with one interior-point iteration per subproblem. Newton steps give a KKT system in which the regularization terms $\rho_{k}$ and $\delta_{k}$ keep the matrix nonsingular for any positive semidefinite $P$. Elimination yields a symmetric quasi-definite augmented system and a positive definite Schur complement with a Cholesky factorization. Each iteration uses predictor-corrector steps with $\tau=0.995$. Termination checks absolute and relative residuals, and the proximal parameters are bounded below for numerical stability.
sections.heading: Preliminaries: Proximal Interior-Point Method for A Single QP
sections.headline: Each iteration solves a Newton system from a proximal interior-point method, using a Mehrotra predictor-corrector step.

sections.body: For learning, the solution is differentiated with respect to the QP data using the implicit function theorem on the optimality residual. The Jacobian is approximated by the forward iteration matrix $J_{k}$, which differs only by regularization terms. The text states these terms are small at the final iteration, which is what justifies the approximation. The adjoint variable $\eta$ solves $J_{k}^{\top}\eta=-\nabla_{\omega}\ell$, and the gradients with respect to $P$, $c$, $A$, $b$, $G$ and $h$ are read from its partitions. Factors from the augmented or Schur system can be reused for this solve; otherwise the matrix is refactorized in the backward pass. For sparse matrices, gradients are gathered only at structural nonzeros.
sections.heading: Differentiation through QPs
sections.headline: Gradients follow from implicit differentiation, with one adjoint solve that reuses the forward iteration matrix.

sections.body: Problem data, iterates, step lengths and per-problem statuses stay in device arrays with a batch dimension. An activity indicator freezes each converged or failed instance, and a device-side reduction decides whether the shared loop continues. Dense problems use the Schur complement with batched Cholesky factorization and cache the product of A with its transpose; matrices smaller than 32 by 32 use shape-specialized kernels. Sparse problems share one pattern in compressed sparse rows, with symbolic analysis done once. The multistage backend uses a parallel method with O(log N) time, compared with O(N) for sequential approaches. Ruiz equilibration is applied, and optional iterative refinement is configurable. Backward passes refactorize instead of storing factors to reduce memory use.
sections.heading: Batched GPU Execution and Implementation
sections.headline: Iteration control stays on the device, and workspaces and factorization structure are reused across solves.

sections.body: Experiments run in float64 on an RTX 5090 GPU and an Intel Ultra 9 285K CPU. cuPIQP is compared with QPAX and Moreau (using cuDSS), and with PIQP and HPIPM on eight pinned CPU cores. QPAX is given a relaxed tolerance of $10^{-4}$ because it struggles at the default accuracy. Batches of up to 16384 QPs come from Franka, G1, G1-with-hands and ALOHA inverse kinematics and whole-body control data. The median iteration counts of both cuPIQP backends are comparable to Moreau and PIQP, so the speedup does not come from fewer iterations. At 16384, QPAX fails on 56 G1 and 215 G1-with-hands problems. PIQP is faster at small batches, while cuPIQP is faster at the largest batch by 1.81×, 2.47×, 1.29× and 4.26× on Franka, G1, G1-with-hands and ALOHA.
sections.heading: Experimental results
sections.headline: On batched robot QP benchmarks, cuPIQP-sparse reaches speedups of up to 18.8× over Moreau.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes cuPIQP as a batched, differentiable GPU QP solver that supports dense, sparse and multistage problems in one framework. It reports solve-time speedups of up to $18.8\times$ over Moreau and $4.26\times$ over eight-core PIQP. In differentiable quadrotor control, it reports end-to-end training speedups of $4.6\times$ over QPAX and $7.8\times$ over Moreau. The stated future work extends the foundation to differentiable sequential quadratic programming for nonlinear model predictive control and other optimization-based applications. The conclusion does not report results for that extension.
sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.headline: cuPIQP is a batched differentiable GPU QP solver for dense, sparse and multistage problems, with nonlinear model predictive control as future work.
